title: Uber Separates Scaling Intent From Execution on Kubernetes Platform
gist: Uber built a ServiceScale CRD and controller so multiple orchestrators (its Up/UDC deployment stack and a failover orchestrator) can safely scale the same Kubernetes workloads, enabling regional failover by borrowing low-tier capacity instead of holding idle reserves. Related work cut steady-state provisioning from 2x to 1.3x and eliminated over one million CPU cores.

insights.claim: Uber's Container Platform runs over 100 compute clusters across data centres and cloud providers including Oracle and Google, with roughly 4,000 services on 3 million cores and 1.5 million daily pod launches.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Scale of Uber's multi-cloud compute footprint and its cloud vendor relationships.

insights.claim: Uber moved from reserving idle capacity in all data centres to scaling down low-tier workloads and scaling up high-tier ones during regional failover.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Reduces compute spend; less idle capacity purchased from providers.
insights.locator: The motivation came from a change

insights.claim: An arXiv paper reports Uber's Unified Failover Architecture reduced steady-state provisioning from 2x to 1.3x and eliminated over one million CPU cores.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Large infrastructure cost savings; negative read-through for cloud capacity demand from such customers.
insights.quote: reduced steady-state provisioning from 2x to 1.3x and eliminated over one million CPU cores

insights.claim: Uber declined to add failover logic to its critical UDC controller because a regression in failover handling could affect normal deployments fleet-wide, instead creating a separate ServiceScale CRD and controller.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Blast-radius isolation as a design principle for critical control planes.
insights.quote: a regression in failover handling wouldn't stay isolated to failover

insights.claim: Uber deliberately avoided an external database, coordination service or separate control plane, materializing scale intent in Kubernetes to keep it debuggable under incident pressure.
insights.speaker: Egor Grishechko and Srikar Paruchuru
insights.so_what: Favors Kubernetes-native designs over added infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: We didn't want an additional external database, a separate coordination service, or a control plane that'd become harder to debug under incident pressure.

insights.claim: Stale informer caches led Uber to add a read-your-own-write guardrail using generation annotations, and Kubernetes v1.36 introduced comparable staleness mitigation for controllers.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Platform-level recognition of multi-writer consistency problems.
insights.locator: The blog post describes three production lessons

insights.claim: Simultaneous updates from UDC and SSC caused ReplicaSet metadata to drift from spec, breaking proportional scaling and sometimes sticking workloads, which Uber handled with fleet-wide drift detection and an automated healer.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Multi-writer control is a real operational risk at scale.

insights.claim: The rollout took a year, supported Kubernetes Deployments and OpenKruise CloneSets, and completed without customer-impacting outages.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Infrastructure changes of this kind are slow, multi-quarter efforts.

insights.claim: The engineers argue multi-orchestrator systems are hard not because of APIs but because of everything that happens between writes.
insights.speaker: Egor Grishechko and Srikar Paruchuru
insights.so_what: Consistency, not interfaces, is the core challenge in multi-controller platforms.
insights.quote: Multi-orchestrator systems aren't hard because of the APIs. They're hard because of everything that happens between writes.

insights.claim: The CNCF graduation of multi-cluster project Karmada and Kubernetes' own staleness mitigation suggest multi-orchestrator problems are gaining platform-level recognition.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Multi-cluster orchestration is maturing as a category.
